text: I'm Charles Ogletree, professor of law at Harvard Law School.  I serve as      lead counsel for the survivors of the 1921 Tulsa Race Riots, one of the      most shocking examples of domestic terrorism in our country's history.

On Capitol Hill today, the aging group will share their memories with      members of the Congressional Black Caucus and others.  Earlier this year,      Ogletree asked the US Supreme Court to allow those who worked and lived      in the Greenwood section of Tulsa to seek reparations from the city and      the state of Oklahoma.  Here again is Charles Ogletree in his own words.

As I reflect on what happened in Tulsa, I'm just amazed      and dismayed at what it would have been to live in Greenwood in the      1920s.  Here was the black Wall Street.  You had black doctors and black      lawyers.  You had black theaters and black hotels.  You had black      churches and black newspapers. You had a community where it's told that a      dollar would circulate 35 times in the community before it left.  That      was a community, despite segregation, despite Jim Crow laws, prosperous,      people who had the level playing field and rose to the top.  It was a      vibrant time in America.

I didn't know about the Tulsa Race Riots until the year      2002, and I was shocked and embarrassed that something that was so      dramatic, so traumatic and so devastating of what was known as the black      Wall Street would be something that escaped me completely.  When I went      to Tulsa for the first time to give a speech in 2002, I learned that on      May 31st, 1921, there was a race riot and that a group of whites had been      deputized by the local sheriff.  They were armed by the local sheriff.      Many of them had been drinking.  And they went into Greenwood, which was      known as the black Wall Street of its time, and they burned down things      like the Stratford Hotel. They burned down the Dreamland Theater.  They      burned down churches, newspapers, all sorts of offices.  They destroyed      homes, and at the end of the day, 8,000 African-Americans were homeless.      Their complete community of 40 square blocks had been destroyed by one of      the worst race riots in our country's history.

I met these survivors, a black woman and man, 89 years      old to 105, who had lived through the 1921 race riots who really had      never told their story and had no opportunity to go to court and have the      evidence presented in a meaningful way, and asked me to represent them.      I agreed to do so, along with many other lawyers, like Johnnie Cochran      and Willie Gary.  It has been for me the most important legal work I've      done in my nearly 30 years as a lawyer, and it's the most significant      work that I've done in terms of trying to give back to a community what      they so richly deserve.

It's very interesting when we think about the issue of      reparations and what we've been willing to do and unwilling to do.  We      correctly were able to steadfastly support the right of reparations of      six million Jews and descendants of those Jews who were exterminated.  It      took decades before anyone recognized the full extent of the harm and      begin to make modest and never adequate compensation.  And it's      important, when we think about reparations, Tulsa should be the poster      child for a clear, unambiguous and compelling case for reparations for      American citizens who lost so much at the hands of the city and the state      government of Oklahoma.

Today is a moment that I've been waiting for for many      years. Finally members of Congress will be holding hearings to allow the      survivors of the Tulsa Race Riots to tell their stories.  So May 10th is      the beginning of a new recognition of what happened in Tulsa and it will      be wonderful when 102-year-old Otis Clark comes into that meeting room      and tells the members of Congress, `I was there.  My family lost their      lives, lost their property.  I survived, and I'm here to tell you that      it's time for justice in Tulsa.'  It's been 84 years, but as he'll say,      `I've lived 102 years to be here today.  I hope you will address this      issue and fix it before I pass on.'

Charles Ogletree is a professor of law at Harvard University.      In the last two years since he filed the lawsuit on behalf of the      survivors of the 1921 Tulsa Race Riots, 36 of them have died.  The      Oklahoma lawsuit seeks no financial payment to survivors or their      families.  Instead it requests the establishment of educational and      health-care resources for current residents of Greenwood.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

I've been      covering Washington events for more than two decades, as a correspondent      for the Chicago Tribune, at one point, and this is--from time to time,      you see these little blips that--as you put it. But for the most part this is an extremely divided House and      Senate, and I don't see at all that there's really movement towards any      kind of bipartisanship that has been traditional.

Charles Ogletree, many are suggesting we are seeing the calm      before the storm, the vote anticipated on Judge Owen today, and there's      still the wrangling over Pryor and Rogers Brown.  We've been talking      about it for the last few weeks on this show.  But people say the big      showdown is going to--and see if there's muster in this alliance--will be      the appointment of eventually a Supreme Court justice.  Do you believe      that to be the case?

That's right, Ed.  This is      just the appetizer.  The main entree is going to be whether or not      Justice Antonin Scalia will be the next chief justice of the Supreme      Court coming this June, and both sides are trying to set themselves up to      make it a viable challenge and a viable nomination.  I think this is an      effort to say, `We can resolve things,' but the real battle will come      when Chief Justice Rehnquist, as we all expect he will, announces his      retirement in late June, and President Bush will likely nominate Antonin      Scalia to be his substitute.  The battle lines will be drawn.  Remember,      Scalia was confirmed 98-to-0 almost 20 years ago in 1986. Senator Harry      Reid from Nevada has already said that he thinks that Scalia's smart and      will be hard to oppose.  Democrats going to have a very hard time, if      Scalia is the nominee, and I think that this coalition of moderation will      not hold when it comes to Supreme Court nominations.

Callie, we were talking about all things being political while      we were off the air.  One of the things that's interesting here is to      take a look at the politicizing of '08, if you will, and I say that in      the true sense--internal politics.  We saw John McCain really draw the      line in the sand.  Bill Frist, I'm sure, did not appreciate what happened      with this alliance.  Is this the Republican Party saying that--to people      in general, `We may not be as far right as you believe'?

Well, certainly John McCain      making himself that way, I mean, making it clear to people that he's      willing to reach out, and I think even though this is a blip--OK?--and I      think we can agree that it probably is a blip, there's something to be      said for some members of Congress finding a spine.  If they don't find a      center, they at least found a spine.  And they have decided to reach      across the aisle even in a limited way. Because they know that their      constituencies are saying, `Hey, people, get something done.'  And I      think that we cannot overlook that this--small, though it may be--this      small step, that it is significant.  It certainly sets up John McCain as      a leader, and, if, after all, leadership is about problem-solving, then      let's give credit to these folks that said, `This is a problem.  We gotta      solve it.  Even if it's not gonna hold for the long term, for now let's      get off the dime.'

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)
text: You're right, Callie.  It's not solved.  And that's the whole      point.  This, more than anything else, was a case of respect for a Senate      tradition, and this is what they want to preserve.  But judging by the      comments on both sides--one, we are not assured they would--this would      not be a showdown later on; and, two, both of them have been soundly      criticized by their respective constituencies.  And so this is far from      being over and you even hear the comments of Frist saying, you know,      `Hey, depends on how they behave.  They act up, we're gonna do--we're      really gonna do what we started to do.'  So this is just a delay; this is      actually not a solution.

But I would say, George, to you, that the larger      constituencies--I mean, that's the folks that voted for people--are--I      think, appreciate some movement.  The special interest constituencies,      yes, you're right, are not happy.  But there's something to be said for      demonstrating to folks, `You put us here to vote on some things, to make      some things happen, and we're at least trying.'
Charles, let me ask...
Well, the question is whether anything is really--OK, go      ahead, Ed.
No--and to pick up on your point--but let me ask you this...

Well, the question is whether anything has happened.      The fact of the matter is that nothing--the same people who the Democrats      opposed two days ago, now they're going to allow to be voted up or down.      So I don't see this as a move toward the center.  I see this as a little      bit of posturing with no real consequence in terms of judicial      nominations, or in terms of broader policy, but we'll wait and see.

Charles, let me ask you this before we move on to another      subject, and that is the idea, as you suggest, if and when Rehnquist      steps down and Scalia takes over, one would believe yet another      ultraconservative will take that spot.  But isn't the key here in terms      of the swing of power and the effect on the country when someone like      Sandra Day O'Connor or a swing vote steps down?  Many anticipate that she      will not necessarily hang on much longer to that seat.

Well, I don't think there's gonna be any equivocation      from President Bush about who he would nominate to the Supreme Court.  He      told us in 1999 before he was elected the first time that his model of a      justice was Clarence Thomas and Antonin Scalia.  He's done nothing to      move from that.  If O'Connor steps down, that's not gonna change his      view.  Remember he promoted Garza--I mean, Estrada, Emilio Estrada.  He      made it clear his vision, and he thinks he has a mandate, so I think the      court's gonna take a strong tilt toward the right, at least in      nominations.
Right.
And the Democrats don't have the votes to block it.  The      president has set up his vision, and I think he'll make sure it's      implemented.
Right.  And that's the point, the idea that replacing a      conservative with a conservative won't be as, in some people's minds,      detrimental as when those swing seats get--all right, let's...

Well, here's the position.  Justice David Souter was      considered a conservative and now he's considered a moderate, and I don't      think President Bush is gonna take a chance on someone who looks like a      Republican, but acts like a Democrat.  He's gonna make sure that he      nominates who he wants, and those are gonna be strongly conservative      candidates for the Supreme Court.

All right, let's move to another subject, and that is--we talked      about it last week--the idea that Newsweek found itself in hot water and      now it's trying to clean it up.  It's announced plans to limit the      magazine's use of anonymous sources following a scandal in which one of      its stories was blamed for a deadly protest in Afghanistan.  That, of      course, is the story about the desecration of the Koran.  And many folks      in the business understand, as often happens, and did in this case,      quote, "unnamed sources were utilized and used to move this story      forward."  When we think, historically, George Curry, there are many,      many stories, including the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal, initially,      obviously, Watergate, that banked on unnamed sources that brought to bear      these stories.  How detrimental, if at all, is this?

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)
text: Well, I don't think it's detrimental, but I don't think      Newsweek went far enough.  What most people will not acknowledge is that      if you're talking about Washington, DC, most of the anonymous sources are      government officials, and I have gone to these briefings at the White      House, for example, where they would bring a Cabinet member on,      and--saying, `Well, you can only use--identify this person as a high      government-ranking official,' and what they're allowed to do is spin      propaganda and not be held accountable.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)
text: So I think Newsweek should have done three things.  One, they should,      first, discontinue the practice of allowing government officials to spin      reporters like that.  I think the rest of the press should do it, as      well.  Two, is if you're gonna use unnamed sources, you should require      somebody to corroborate that information.  And, thirdly, we should be      going to the government to approve stories in advance, which is what they      did here.  That bothers me and so does--two years ago, the news director      for CNN went to the Pentagon to say, `We're thinking about using these      generals to comment on the war.  Are they OK with you?'  I mean, this is,      to me going--Newsweek, in this instance, showed it to two government      officials.  You're allowing them to, quite basically, publish your      magazine, and, I think, I'm just as offended by that as I am anything      else.

I have to underscore what George has said.  I want to pull      out the part about corroboration.  People bring up Watergate all the time      as an example of unnamed sources, but they fail to also articulate that      after they got the first information, they had to go and corroborate      that, and that is what is the key.  Now journalism leaders are saying,      over and over, there has got to be some more transparency of the kind      that George just articulated, or you've got to corroborate that      information, and that'll cut off a lot of these, quote, unquote,      "mistakes."
Though Newsweek will argue that this was part of their      corroboration process here, in the fact that they didn't just go on this.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)
text: No, they...
Well, they...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

One source, yes.  One governmental source, yes.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

But...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Exactly.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Well, I don't know that they have a higher standard.      Come on now.  I mean...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

No, oh--now come on now.
Let's be honest.  They're supposed to.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Right, right.  And they don't want to be scooped.
They're supposed to.  And, I mean--and, then, George--and there      it is, George.
They don't want to be scooped.

Michael Isikoff and John Barry who were writers of this      particular article have suggested--and this is what I was talking      about--that they sought comment from two Defense Department officials. And, in fact, I'm sure they felt pressured to move this story rather      than continue the process of trying to find another corroboration.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Yeah, but professional...

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Yes.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Well--and Professor Ogletree, professional journalists      have a standard by which their work is governed. All right.

Well, I'm not trying to equate this with bloggers.  What      I'm saying is that Newsweek wanted to get this story out.  They did get      it out. They made a mistake. That's true.

Oh-ho!

Yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. GEORGE CURRY (Editor In Chief, National Newspaper Publishers      Association News Service)

Yes, I understand the pressure, but the difference is that      all we have, professional journalists, is our credibility, and that rests      in corroboration and sourcing.  The difference is what I tell college      students all the time.  Anybody can throw anything up on the Internet and      say it's information I've gathered.  But where did it come from?  How can      you prove to me that it's something that's reliable?  That is the      difference in the work of professional journalists.

Let me just ask you, Callie--let's just watch this.      Who's going to be fired from Newsweek, who's going to be punished.      What's going to be the consequences?  If you tell me that this is going      to be like CBS where they're going to clean house because of a story that      couldn't be corroborated, then I'll agree with you.  If business goes on      with the simple retraction, and no one's held accountable, I don't see      the higher standard if there's no consequence for reporting a story that      cannot be corroborated.

Well, let me say this.  There is a higher standard.  Now      whether or not people suffer at the high hands of it in this instance is      another question, and I take your point, except to say that there is vast      numbers of other professional journalists doing the job every day,      meeting the higher standard and whether or not Newsweek cleans house does      not determine whether or not the rest of us go about the business of      trying to source and corroborate in the way that we know, makes capital J      journalism what it is.

And--but, you know, I think      it's, in the end, good because it's a healthy discussion and it does      raise questions about how we use anonymous sources, and that is a problem      that needs to be addressed.

All right, well, we got into such a healthy discussion, we      couldn't get to our other two matters today.  But Callie Crossley,      Charles Ogletree, George Curry, I thank you so much for what is a very      entertaining--or has been a very entertaining and, I hope, informative      Roundtable.

Over the weekend, Chief Justice William Hubbs Rehnquist died at his home      in Virginia.  He was 80.  And today, President Bush nominated Judge John      Roberts to replace him.  Roberts was previously nominated to replace      retiring Justice Sandra Day O'Connor.  Joining us to talk about the      court's 16th chief justice and African-Americans are Harvard law      Professor Charles Ogletree and Ted Shaw, president and director-counsel      for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.
Gentlemen, thank you so much and welcome.
Hello, Farai.  Good to      be with you.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Thank you.  Good to be with you.

So we want to spend some time on the legacy of Justice      Rehnquist, but first, let's ask the big question:  Why has Judge Roberts,      who until today was just a nominee for an associate justice, been so      swiftly moved to the front of the line for chief justice?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, I think it makes sense from the administration's point      of view.  They wanted to have somebody in place by the first Monday in      October, when the court begins its new term.  And they don't want the      court coming into session without new leadership that they have chosen.      If they did not replace Chief Justice Rehnquist, then Justice Stevens      would be the acting chief justice.  I don't think that's something they      want, and they don't want the vacancy, period.  In terms of Justice      Roberts' re-nomination for chief justice, it's not really a surprise.  I      think that there were three options. One was to elevate one of the      current sitting associate justices.  The other was to nominate somebody      fresh to be chief.  But John Roberts is a known quantity, he's been      vetted, and they have a lot of confidence in his intellectual ability,      and he's going to be on the court for 30 years, if he's confirmed, as      chief now.  So for them, it's a move that I think has a lot of logic to      it.

Let's talk a little bit about the special role of the chief      justice. What, in fact is the--obviously all of the Supreme Court      justices are incredibly powerful in shaping legal policy, but what does      the chief justice do?

I think some people overstate and others understate the      role of the chief justice.  One of the most important roles, of course,      if he or she is in the majority and if an opinion--they choose who will      write the actual opinion.  That's a very important, substantive piece of      power.  Chief Justice Rehnquist had an important role in that he has      changed the court's role dramatically from what it was when he joined the      court.  The court was hearing probably 160 or more cases in the '70s and      that--he's cut that number down to about 80 cases a year.  So they really      are very selective on what they hear, which means a lot of cases that      many people may think have merit will never get any attention before the      Supreme Court.

But other thing that's important, and Chief Justice Rehnquist did this      with great class and with great effect:  He really spoke strongly about      the importance of the independence of the federal judiciary, seeking pay      raises for judges who ironically--some federal judges are making less      money than my law students who graduate after being at a law firm and go      into private practice, and that's a serious concern.  But it also helps      to set the tone for the court in terms of where it's going to go.  Given      John Roberts' record as a judge and as a lawyer, it clearly will make      this court swing even further to the right than it might have been with      Chief Justice Rehnquist.  And my only quibble with my dear friend Ted      Shaw is that I think Roberts will serve not 30 years but perhaps 40.      With the changes in health and age and all of that, he will be there for      a very, very long time, and he will have a major impact on the direction      of the court as we look forward.

Charles, let me just ask you--I don't want to go too deep into      talking about Judge Roberts before we get to Rehnquist, but you say that      he, as a chief justice, will swing the court further right.  What makes      you believe that?

His record, his disposition, his views, his      associations, his opinions, the memoranda that he's written, whether in      the solicitor general's office or working in the White House or any other      capacity.  He has been consistently, unequivocally conservative in every      time he's expressed his points of view.  And there isn't a whole lot of      equivocation there.  Now he has a right to be conservative, and President      Bush won the election; he has the right to appoint him.  But we shouldn't      be fooled in thinking that Roberts is going to be anything different than      a conservative, based on his views about federalism, his views about      affirmative action, his views about Roe vs. Wade.  And our hope is that      he will follow the law as it has been established and not see this as an      opportunity to swing more decisively to the right.  But we shouldn't be      fooled.  He's a conservative.  That's who President Bush wanted to      appoint and that's who he has appointed, and that's who will be, I think,      the chief justice come October 3rd, 2005.

I want to lead both of you gentlemen through the legacy of      Chief Justice Rehnquist.  Let me start with you, Ted.  When William      Rehnquist was nominated as an associate justice to the bench by Nixon in      1971, there were questions about his role as director for the Republican      Party's Operation Eagle Eye, what was called a ballot security program.      Tell us a little bit, if you can, about what that was.  And was it      appropriate for a judge to be involved in that?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, there were questions about William Rehnquist's role in      monitoring voters in Phoenix, where he was in private practice, and there      were charges that he intimidated voters along with others.  And all of      that is in the record now, and I'm not sure this is the time to go back      and rehash all that.  I'll just say that Chief Justice Rehnquist has been      remarkably consistent over the years, from the time he was a law clerk      through the time you're talking about when he was in private practice,      through his time on the bench.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: I perhaps have one difference with my good friend, Charles Ogletree,      which is I'm not sure that John Roberts will actually be any more      conservative than Chief Justice Rehnquist was.  He was very conservative,      although I think that during John Roberts' time on the court, if he's      confirmed, we may see the court move even further to the right as      President Bush gets another appointment in addition to his, and there's      always the possibility of more appointments.  But Chief Justice      Rehnquist's vote was one that we at the Legal Defense Fund would have      been happy to have, but in almost every circumstance in major civil      rights cases, we didn't get that vote.  Now there were a few cases in      which he came our way.  The Miranda decision was widely expected by some      conservatives to be overruled.  Chief Justice Rehnquist did not go along      with that.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: But for the most part, he was a very difficult vote for us to get, but he      certainly had a tremendous impact on the court, on the jurisprudence.  He      started as an outlier when he was appointed to the court.  By the end of      his life, he was right there in control of a very conservative court that      may get to be even more conservative.
Ted, let me follow up and ask you about the affirmative action      cases that the chief justice ruled on.  How did he vote in the various      affirmative action cases that came before him?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, he was a reliable vote against affirmative action.  Most      recently in the Michigan cases, he certainly expressed his opposition to      affirmative action, although in one of the opinions, his position wasn't      as clear as perhaps it had been in some of the earlier cases.  But he      generally was very suspicious of affirmative action, if not antagonistic      to it, and that was consistent through--even before Michigan, the      contracting cases that were before the Supreme Court, the Adarand case      involving federal contracting and the Croson case involving the municipal      contracting in the city of Richmond. Although Justice O'Connor was seen      as the swing vote, obviously this was a Rehnquist court, and he was a      formidable intellect.  So what he said had had effect.

Let me ask you, Charles, about minority clerks.  Judge      Rehnquist never hired a single African-American among the 82 clerks that      he had; 81 of those 82 were white, and he said, you know, `Wait for the      demographics to change.  There's no need for a wider net.  The system is      working just fine.' In your role as a Harvard law professor, do you find      that acceptable?  Do you find it acceptable that this pathway to the      inner workings of the justice system is--has essentially been for many of      the justices...

Well, let me say--answer this way:  Regrettably, Chief      Justice Rehnquist was not the only Supreme Court justice to not hire      African-American clerks.  And, in fact, some of our liberal friends who      served on the courts in earlier times also did not hire African-American      clerks.  The good news is, despite what Rehnquist has said and failed to      do, is that many members of the court, from Justice Stevens and Justice      Breyer, in particular Justice O'Connor, other judges have hired      African-American clerks, and it's a much better day.  I've had a number      of students who are exceptional.  They're not, you know, special admits      or special qualified folks.  They're really brilliant students, and I'm      glad that the court is having a little bit more diversity.

But that is a problem because you want the court to look like America.      You want the law school to look like America.  You want the law firms to      look like America, and that's one of the disappointments.

About Rehnquist, though, let me just say this about the legacy.  First of      all, when he was initially ill, I sent a leader to him expressing my deep      regrets about my illness, and I sent my condolences out to his family      now.  He was a very brilliant man.  He was number one in his his class at      Stanford.  He actually wrote a brilliant essay for a book that Deborah      Rhode at Stanford and I co-edited called "Brown @ 50," talking      about--praising Earl Warren, who wrote the unanimous decision in Brown      vs. Board of Education in 1950.  He handled the impeachment hearings of      President Clinton with excellence.  His public scholarship on the courts      and society were phenomenal.

But Ted is right; his decisions is where it made a difference.  He was      the Lone Ranger.  He was out there in dissent.  He wrote--he was in the      majority in Bush vs. Gore that stopped the vote in Florida in 2000,      against affirmative action in the Michigan case, one of the two      dissenters in Roe vs. Wade.  He has carefully and effectively over the      last 33 years cut back on exclusionary rule, given police more power and      suspects less power.  And when it comes to racial profiling, people have      to be very concerned that the court has moved in a very, very      conservative area that provides less protection for people than before.      So that's part of the legacy.  It's a mixed legacy, but when it comes to      issues of race and justice, I think folks are going to be less      congratulatory and more critical.  But the overall legacy will be shaped      up as someone who stuck by his views over a very, very long period of      time.

Let me ask you about whether or not the Bush administration is      going to feel pressure to nominate a woman or a person of color or both      for Sandra Day O'Connor's seat.  Sandra Day O'Connor herself expressed      some dismay that a woman was not nominated.  Now that Judge Roberts is      being nominated for the supreme Supreme seat, if you'd put it that way,      is the Bush administration going to feel pressure to take a second look      at the diversity of the court?

I think they'll feel pressure, but that means nothing.      Laura Bush appealed to him.  The Hispanic community appealed to President      Bush and he seemed to be taking those views into consideration, but he      nominated John Roberts, not Edith Clement, not Alberto Gonzales.  So I      think there will be pressure, but he doesn't have to run again, and he      wants to formalize his legacy as a president.  And I think even though      there will be pressure, that won't ultimately influence his choice.

I think what's interesting is that if the Roberts hearing, since it's      been elevated, is as contentious and as demanding as we anticipate, we      may see on Monday, October 3rd, Justice Sandra Day O'Connor as the ninth      justice, and she will serve until there's a replacement.  That's not a      bad thing for her to continue in that role, but I think that ultimately      the president will nominate a second person, and I hope that he does look      at the court and make sure that his legacy, as he claims it was in Texas,      as he promised it would be in the White House, as he's done with Colin      Powell and Condoleezza Rice and Alberto Gonzales and others--that the      court will look much more diverse with talented people who are diverse in      gender and ethnicity, and that should mean that someone, unlike the men      who are white on the court, will join the court and add some diversity      sometime after October.
Ted, what do you think the chances are for more diversity on      the court?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, I think that there will be some pressure in the minds of      some to appoint a Latino or a woman, a Latina, or something like that,      but I agree with Charles.  I don't think that the president is going to      feel a lot of that pressure.  He's going to appoint whom he wants to      appoint.  In my view, my concern isn't so much whether we have a Latino,      another African-American or a woman.  That's important.  I don't mean to      say that it's not, but I want somebody on the court who, although they're      conservative, is fair, open-minded, whose vote is in play, who will hear      the arguments, who does not come to the court with a mission-driven      agenda.  That's what the Legal Defense Fund said we wanted with respect      to the Roberts nomination. It's what we want with respect to any justice.      That's important.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: I do want to take this moment, though, to say that we also send out our      condolences on a personal level to the Rehnquist family.  Whatever      disappointments we had with getting the chief justice's vote, this is a      time for us to recognize that they've suffered a loss and the nation is      in mourning, and we join folks in sending condolences.

Let me--We're running out of time now--just ask a broader      question, which is, you two gentlemen, obviously, are legal experts,      legal scholars, and legal issues have always been inextricably tied to      the advancements of African-Americans in this country.  How important is      it for ordinary citizens to understand these decisions that the court      makes?  They're always very complicated and they flash across the front      pages.  What can people do to better educate themselves about these      decisions?

Farai, I think that's the most important question,      because we keep thinking that the Supreme Court is this high and supreme      entity that's removed from the people.  But I remember a slogan--I think      it's in the Florida Supreme Court--that said:  The court is where the      injured flock for justice. And I think the court is very important in      every aspect of our lives.  Our rights of privacy, whether we're going to      be taxed, whether we can get an education or a job, whether we face      discrimination.

And so even though those 80 decisions may not impact us every single day      in every single way, the court does enact the supreme law of the land,      and I think that we need to see it as more important.  We knew before      November 2004 that whoever became president would select two, three or      maybe even four Supreme Court justices by 2009, when the term officially      ends for the presidency.  So it's very important and it affects our      everyday lives.  Cases like what's going to happen to the tragedy that's      going on in the Gulf Coast and Florida and Alabama and Louisiana and      Mississippi now--that's going to come before the court in some way;      questions about whether or not the terrorism concern that's of      international concern will have some domestic impact on people's rights      of privacy.

All right.  I'm going to have to stop you there.      Unfortunately, Ted, I don't have another second.  I just want to thank      you both so much.  We are going to obviously keep on this story of the      Supreme Court as it evolves. Ted Shaw, president and director-counsel for      the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, and Charles Ogletree, law professor at      Harvard University.  Thank you, gentlemen, for joining us.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.
This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Ed Gordon.

On today's roundtable, racial segregation is no longer permitted in      California prisons and two officers caught on tape pay the price.      Joining us today to discuss these topics is Julianne Malveaux.  She's an      economist and author and also president and CEO of Last Word Productions.      She joins us from Washington, DC.  From our New York bureau, Michael      Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition.  And      Charles Ogletree, Harvard law professor, joins us from Harvard University      studios there in Cambridge, Mass.
Thank you all for joining us.  Greatly appreciate it.

Let me start with something--and, Michael Meyers, I'll go directly to      you--in relation to what we are also seeing, offshoots of this      transportation strike if you will.  We are now seeing race interjected,      surprise, surprise, in the transit strike debate.  The mayor in a press      conference yesterday used the word thugs when talking about the actions      of the union.  We are now seeing some City Council members and religious      leaders in New York City suggesting that this had racial overtones.      There are others who are saying, `Ah, you're going a little bit too far.      The term thugs historically has been used when talking about unions in      our history here in the United States.'  How do you think that plays      itself out, Michael Meyers?  Is that being too sensitive in your opinion?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I think it's ridiculous.  I think it's just race baiting.  It's--I don't      have any beef with Mayor Bloomberg.  I really don't.  I don't like the      man, but, look, thuggish behavior is thuggish behavior.  You have people      who have gone out on an awful strike against the public interest that      involves the safety of New Yorkers--home-care workers who cannot get to      their senior citizens who are shut up in the outer boroughs.  So, yeah,      there was no need for this strike, but it's going--I see the end is near      not because of racial breast-beating of these racial arsonists but      because the judge has said, `Jail is now an option and personal fines are      an option.'  This is near the end.

Charles Ogletree, let me ask you this.  From a legal      perspective, when you start to hear the term imprisonment in negotiations      like this, have you seen historically that it does weaken the resolve of      those out on picket lines?

Not at all, Ed, and      sometimes it reinforces it.  These workers are fighting for a decent      wage, decent pension, a quality of life, and they know in order to fight      for what's right for workers, they're going to suffer risk of fines,      suffer possible imprisonment, suffer being subjected to derogatory terms      like thugs or other terms that Michael used.  And I think that, you know,      as much as I have relatives and friends who are deeply inconvenienced by      this strike, I understand the broader issues at stake.  And if there were      the right sort of wages, there were the right quality of life, this would      have been settled long ago.  And I think we're going to see both a      reasonable settlement and an end to the strike but not until a step      forward.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: But, Professor, you don't live in New York.  These people      are very comfortable.
You know what, Michael?
I don't have to live in New York, Michael.  That's not      the point.  Come on.  This...

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: These people are very comfortable.  You don't drive our      subways and buses.
Look, you know what?  I lived in the last...
Let me stop us for just a moment.  Julianne Malveaux...
Let's stop the regional baitings.

...the reason I--let me ask this question.  I'm coming to you      today from my hometown.  I'm home for the holidays, WDET here in Detroit,      making a fine home for us this week.  But let me ask you this as it      relates to the race-baiting question and then pick up on your point.  One      of the things I heard before I left New York is that there was concern      because the Transportation Workers Union president, Roger Toussaint, is a      man of color that you weren't going to see perhaps the same kind of      solidarity that historically you have seen from the streets of New York      and that that in and of itself sometimes when a black face is the forward      face, it has an adverse effect on how people see it.

You know, I think that that's something to consider, Ed.      At the same time, I lived through the last strike.  It was 11 days and it      went 11 days.  And there was a settlement.  People made do.  Yes, it was      inconvenient. Here's the sticking point on this strike.  It's the      pension.  It's not the wages.  The wage increases that the union was      asking for was modest and what MTA is offering is modest, I think 3, 3.5      and 4 percent, a total of about 10.5 percent.  That is very modest, but      the fact is that all those wage increases will be wiped out if the      pension contribution has to go up.  And that's the thing we have to look      at.  Unions now, as you know coming from Detroit, are more      disproportionately black and brown than they've ever been, but      African-American men and women especially gain more percentagewise by      being a union than by being unorganized.  Whites gain as well, and so the      solidarity issue will be there.  If anybody needs to go to jail, Michael      Meyers, it's those MTA officers who have the temerity to take an issue      that did not belong on the bargaining table and put it there.  That's who      needs to be jailed, and that's where the racism lies.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: I don't believe this is racism at all.  I think this is      arrogant...
Well, I know you never believe it's racism, Michael.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Just a second.  I think this is arrogance.  This is...
I mean, the Klan can come by your house and you wouldn't      disagree with them.
Julianne, hold on.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: ...arrogance on the part of the union and, yes, it's      arrogance on the part of the MTA.  If I would the governor, I would      require the chairman of the MTA to resign.  I would require that in order      to settle this strike, there will be no negotiations until people are      back to work.  If I were the judge, I'd say, `Jail!'  And if I were the      people who were in power, I would say, `No amnesty in terms of fines.'      People would run back to work.  They are accountable.
All right.  Hard-liner, let me bring it back to something...
Not necessarily.

...that Julianne raised and, Charles Ogletree, pick it up for      me.  If we take this as a microcosm, one of the things that we're seeing      in the United States across the board quite frankly is the change in what      used to be very solid a foundation if you will and that is the pension      fund system across the boards.  And as Julianne alluded to just a moment      ago, not only with this strike but all of the changes we're seeing across      the country, will disproportionately affect people of color in this      country.

That's true.  It's the lifeline.  When you talk about      quality of life and wondering what your life's going to be like when you      can't work or are unable to work in your declining years, you work now      with the hope that there'll be a cushion to help you live down the road.      And so these things are not just about whether or not you get another      dollar or another day of leave. It's whether or not you have a quality of      life when you can no longer work and pension is essential.  If you look      at private industry, it's very important. If you look at every other      industry, it's very important and these workers deserve that basis.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Nobody's taking their pensions away in New York.

I want to just kind of want Julianne's point.  I didn't      finish my point.  Let me finish my point.  The issue of racism is      complicated as well because, you know, we all know Bill Lucy who is a      very prominent African-American, been involved in labor for decades and      nationally respected. I think it's the changing face of the union      movement.  That's a good thing; that it is becoming more inclusive, it's      becoming more representative of the workers of the nation.  And I think      that ultimately will--with more black mayors, with more black public      officials, I hope that will help down the road as well to make sure that      folks who are rising in these positions will be able to make sure that      those who work for them get a quality of life.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Professor...
You know what?  The other piece of this, Ed Gordon, is...

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: ...you should not mistake the facts.  The pensions are not      an issue in New York.
The pensions were put on the table, Michael.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: People can retire--present workers...
No, the pensions were put on the table as you know.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: ...can retire at the age of 55.
But the pensions were put on the table and they did not      belong there.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: The only issue is whether or not...
All right.  All right.  Guys, listen, we are not going to bang      out...

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: ...(unintelligible) contributions for the new workers.
...negotiations for the MTA on the show today.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: That's right.
So let me move to something else that has hit the wires here.
Ed, let me just say one little tiny point if I might.
Real quick, Julianne.  Real quick.

You know, the other issue is that these pensions are part      of the deferred compensation.  Unions have been very reasonable in the      past because there have been pension contributions.  So it's highly      unfair to go back after the fact and say, `We want to take that away.'
Right.
All right.  And that continues to be the rub in all of this and      we're seeing that happen more and more across this country.

All right.  Let me move to headlines, and again, Charles Ogletree, I'll      go and defer to your legal expertise here.  We are seeing that two of the      police officers involved in the videotaped beating of the victim that so      many of us saw infamously being brutalized by officers, a 64-year-old      Robert Davis, have been fired by the New Orleans police force.  The union      is vowing to fight the firing of these two officers, suggesting that the      media frenzy surrounding all of this made it impossible for them to      receive a fair hearing.  We should note that a third officer has been      suspended for 120 days and three others will face trial January 11th for      various charges.  That being said, when you hear something like media      frenzy making it impossible to get a fair hearing, we hear that kind of      defense all the time, Charles Ogletree.  How realistic is that, one, and      how do you see that in this instance?

Well, here it's not media frenzy.  The videotape tells      the story and it tells it in a very powerful way.  Here was a non-violent      innocent individual walking the streets and being brutally beaten.  And I      think the action taken is a modest measure but an important step in the      right direction. And I think it sends a message that what might have gone      on in New Orleans or in South Central Los Angeles or in New York or in      any other place before just won't be tolerated.  And what's great is that      the objection to this beating were not along racial lines.  Every person      who saw it said, `This is just incomprehensible and certainly can't in      any way justify it.'  So I think it's an important first step.

I'm very interested in not what the New Orleans Police Department is      doing, but I'm worry about the federal role 'cause there were federal      officers involved in this.  And I think we should not see this first step      as a conclusion to the problems of misconduct.  It gets deeper and larger      and I hope that will be coming to the public eye and the press will help      bring this to the public eye as we go forward.

We should note also, Michael Meyers, that a federal civil rights      investigation has been launched through all of this.  And I'm curious,      Michael, your take on here is yet another, even if you include the      extenuating circumstances of the time in New Orleans during Katrina,      videotaped beating of the--brutalizing of an African-American male.  This      seems to not go away. This happens quite frankly daily in this country.      When are we going to see the ire of the community as it was in Rodney      King to try to finally put stopgap measures across the board to assist in      stopping this kind of action?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, you have such measures in place in some cities and      locales. And you have departmental trials for officers who break the      rules.  And you have federal prosecutions of people who violate your      civil rights.  And in some states, you have civil complaint review      boards.  And in most places, you have internal trials, where the police      commissioner or whoever's in charge of the police department has a right      to discipline the officers and fire them for misconduct.  So--but, you      know, when you say, `Let's go to the videotape,' you can't then just      say--cry it's media bias.  Here, I agree with the professor. The issue of      crime is something that usually is raised in a court of law in terms of      prejudicial impact on the right to the defendant.  This was an internal      departmental situation.  The police commissioner or chief, in my      judgment, had the videotape proof, and there was virtually little to no      defense.  And so they're out and out for good, and I say good.

Julianne, pick up on that point.  Both Michael and Professor      Ogletree have suggested that the sense of media frenzy does not pass      muster here.  Do you buy that?  Or is there any indication that can be      used by the defense in suggesting that, while it looks bad, the idea that      it was played over and over and over and over again makes it      impossible--impossible--to find a way to defend the use of police      officers?

I think it's impossible to find a way to defend behavior      that's indefensible.  It has nothing whatsoever to do with the media.      The only thing I would say is to step back for a moment and look at what      I would consider the trickle-down dehumanization of the black people of      New Orleans that happened in the wake of Katrina.  First you heard these      rumors of rapes and lootings that were not taking place.  Then you had      our government literally abandon people for five days.  Then you had      these police officers behaving--the Red Cross didn't go because they      thought it was too dangerous.  They did collect money but they didn't go      because they thought it was too dangerous.  And then you had these police      officers either, A, walking off the job or, B, walking around in, you      know, crazy stress because they thought everybody was a lunatic or a      murderer.

And so you had a trickle-down dehumanization, a climate of      dehumanization, in New Orleans at that time.  This is no excuse, but I      think we have to look not only at these officers and at the police chief,      and my only question would be: Why did it take so long?  I mean, this      happened, you know, in early September. Here we are at the end of the      year, and these folks have been coasting.  Why did it take so long?  But      why, still, do we have evacuees who don't have anywhere to live?  Again,      the term I would use is this is trickle-down dehumanization, the notion      that black life is cheap.
I would just have a difference...

Here's the interesting point.  Here's the interesting point.      Pick up, Charles, but here's the interesting point in that:  If you buy      Julianne's assertion that there was this dehumanization, much of that,      quite frankly, in the first few days when we heard about the stories she      talked about, were being told by black police officers and officials in      the city of New Orleans, as well.

Well, but I think the larger point is that we had a      media interest and focus on New Orleans when it was a `gotcha' story.      What I worry about now is that we have media amnesia.  People think that      the issue has been resolved.  There's suffering in New Orleans; tens of      thousands of people who can't come back home.  The Ninth Ward is      devastated.  Jobs are not being given in proportionate numbers to      African-Americans who want and need to work.  And I think the media is      sort of--there's no picture of a crying baby, there's no picture of a      single mom, there's no picture of someone on a rooftop, and so now there      is little interest in New Orleans.  And I think this is the most critical      period of New Orleans, where we have to worry about both Donald Trump and      Donald Duck finding a place in New Orleans for entertainment and      development, and not thinking about how to rebuild this community for the      natural residents.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well...
So I hope our focus will be on media interest and not      media amnesia about one of the greatest natural disasters in our      country's history.

Lest we forget, Michael Meyers, one of the things that we saw      FEMA get smart about, and the government in general, is extending, at      least through the holidays, the stay of many of these evacuees who      continue to live in government-subsidized hotels but have no real      prospects for housing when these terms are up, which will happen in      January and February.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, since we're switching the topic from police brutality      to the issues of social justice and generally speaking...
Would you like to stay with police brutality, Michael Meyers?      If that floats your boat, I'm in a giving mood during the holiday season.
Ed, you know he likes police brutality.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Excuse me, Julianne.  I deplore police brutality as much as      I deplore racial rhetoric really which comes from the likes of racial      arsonists. Now let me say this about social justice.  You know, like in      the US Senate and the Congress we've seen just very recently, you know,      as Meg Greenfield said many years ago, we used to have a war against      poverty in this nation.  Now we've substituted a war against the poor and      the people who are the most vulnerable--the homeless, the vulnerable, the      sick, the affirmed.  The very poor.  They need governmental subsistence      and support. speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)

And in her opinions on the second circuit, she hasn't had much opportunity, and most lower court judges don't have much opportunity to articulate what the appropriate role of a judge is. So I think it is important to consider what she said about the judicial role when she has been speaking outside of the courtroom, and she said many of these statements time and time again over a number of years.

Let's bring Charles Ogletree into the conversation, and your signature was among more than 1,000 of law professors across the country endorsing Sonia Sotomayor. Why do you think the Senate should vote to confirm her?

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Well, because she's exceptionally well-qualified. I've known Judge Sotomayor for a long time. She's hired some of my students as law clerks. I've read her opinions, and the reality is that if you listen - I was there today at the hearings. It's amazing that it's very hard to find an opinion that she's written or been a part of, out of 3,000, that you can say - or any opinion where she says as a Latina woman or as a woman or as a minority, I feel this way. She doesn't do that.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: In fact, she is very pedantic about the law, respects the law and constantly says in cases like the crash of the TWA airplane with their, you know, victims, innocent victims, that she couldn't side with them because the law didn't allow it. She always cites precedent. Even in the Ritchie case, which people have talked about, she was going with the existing law.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: So she is someone who is not only mainstream but moderate in her decisions, and I think that that's what the senators are finding out, and I'm glad that people are testifying. They have a right to say what they want to say. They ask the questions, and she has an obligation to answer them, even if the answer is I can't comment on it. But I think at the end of the day, 70 or more of these senators will say, you know what? She's qualified. There's no qualification that excludes her, and we should confirm her.
Seventy or more. What do you think the vote is going to be on the Judiciary Committee?

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: I think it'll be over a dozen.
And that would include, of course, well, there are 12 Democrats, so…

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Yup.
So you think they're going to get some Republicans.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Yes, and I won't name them, not yet.
David Savage, what do you think of Charles Ogletree's prognostications there?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: Well, it may be right. I do not have any idea. All the Republicans have asked skeptical questions. I don't know, in the end, whether some of them will vote for her. I do think a lot of - their feeling is that, you know, Barack Obama voted against John Roberts and Sam Alito. The vote against Sam Alito was pretty much of a partisan line. I think the Republicans think they could all line up and vote against her.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: I don't sense that any of them are particularly - I don't think anybody's going after her too hard. So I can also imagine a couple saying, we'll vote for her, and then we'll hold our fire for President Obama's next nominee.

And there is that well-known quote, Charles Ogletree, about the - President Obama, when deciding his vote, eventually against John Roberts, telling his chief of staff at the time, well, you know, if I were to appoint a Supreme Court nominee, I wouldn't want people making the decision simply on the basis of ideology and his chief of staff saying, well, politics tells you to vote against her.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Yeah, I think Barack Obama has made a wise set of choices in those who he's opposed as a senator and now who he's nominated for the Supreme Court, and he was right about Roberts and about Alito.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: They have not just been conservatives, but in fact, if you look at Alito's opinion the Ritchie case and other cases, he'd like to move the ball even further in terms of the importance of Title VII of the - 1964 Civil Rights Act. And I think that even Barack Obama, when he talked about the issue of empathy, I hope that's something I taught him in law school. That's a good thing. It's not liberal. It's not conservative.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: It's a sense of understanding people and putting yourself in that position to understand them, but it's not saying that's how you're going to decide a case, but you decide it with a sense of bringing your experience in there. And Judge Sotomayor has appropriately backed off of that and have some people concerned. But the reality is she's right, and her opinions are what make a difference.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: I'd like someone to say in these 3,000 opinions, she is going to be a liberal or more liberal than the court now. In fact, I'm, as a supporter, very concerned about her criminal justice opinions. She's been siding with the government in very serious cases, and I haven't seen her at all go beyond what the law requires to give someone extra benefit or extra credit.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: So she's a very tough-minded jurist, very well-prepared jurist. And she will be, I think, a suitable opponent for people like Justice Scalia, who I admire, when she joins the court.

Neomi Rao, Judge Sotomayor, as part of that background she sites, is of course as a prosecutor in the Manhattan district attorney's office. And as we just heard from Professor Ogletree, she has sided often with the prosecution side of the case in her role as a judge.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: I think that that's right. I think it's often hard, though, to evaluate a judge's philosophy simply by the outcome of a case, right? I mean, we have to look at what the underlying law is, how they approach the current precedent and how they're applying the law to the specific facts of a case. And I think it's interesting.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: She has espoused, you know, a fidelity to the law, and she said repeatedly over the last few days that she wants to follow the law and not her heart, which is a comment that President Obama had made. But of course, in having fidelity to the law, there are a number of ways that people can do that.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: There are many different approaches to being faithful to the law, and I think what we haven't seen in the hearing is her articulating just how she would approach statutes and the Constitution in the process of interpreting them.
Do you think that she would be different or decidedly different from the justice that she would be replacing, David Souter?

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: I think that's hard to predict. It's always hard to say how someone is going to decide cases once they're on the Supreme Court. I think most indications are that she would probably agree with Justice Souter in a large number of cases, but that, of course, isn't the test for whether someone should be confirmed.

And the empathy that you're talking about that was the standard raised by President Obama, in 95 percent of the cases, he said, well, it's the law. The last few cases, he said, well, somebody's life experience really does make a difference. That has become really, well, a very important word in the debates that we've been hearing over the past few days.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: I think that's right, and I think in part that's because there are very few politicians who are willing to espouse this kind of personal approach to judging. I mean, I think senators on both sides of the political spectrum at least say repeatedly that we want judges who make law, not policy, and…
The umpire analogy.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: The umpire analogy. Almost everyone agrees with that as a matter of theory or in the abstract, even if perhaps they intend different things by it when they use those words. So I think what's so interesting about President Obama's statement is that it really is outside of the accepted rhetoric about the judicial role.

And we've just been mentioning the umpire analogy. We heard excerpts today, Judge Sonia Sotomayor being asked questions, some tough questions by Republican senators. And well, there were some questions from the Democratic side of the aisle, indeed more questions from the Democratic side of the aisle than the Republican side, given the lopsided majority the Democrats enjoy on the Judiciary Committee of 12 to seven, but they were not especially challenging. Here, for example, Ben Cardin, the Democrat from the state of Maryland.

I just want you to know that the baseball fans of Baltimore knew there was a judge somewhere that changed, in a very favorable way, the reputation of Baltimore forever. You are a hero, and they now know it's Judge Sotomayor. You're a hero to the Baltimore fan - baseball fans. Let me explain. The Major League Baseball strike, you allowed the season to continue so Carl Ripken could become the iron man of baseball in September 1995.
So we just want to invite you - as a baseball fan, we want to invite you to an Oriole game, and we promise it will not be when the Yankees are playing so you can root for the Baltimore Orioles.

speaker_label: Judge SONIA SOTOMAYOR (Second Circuit Court of Appeals; Supreme Court Nominee)
text: That's a great invitation. And good morning, Senator. You can assure your Baltimore fans that I have been to Camden Yards. It's a beautiful stadium.

And other very controversial matters. Probably the endorsement of the New York Yankees the most controversial thing she has said in her hearings so far these last couple of days. What do we learn in these hearings, Charles Ogletree?

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Well, one thing. I don't everybody got the memo. The memo that went around made clear Barack Obama is not a candidate for the Supreme Court. What he says, what he believes is irrelevant. Sonia Sotomayor's writings are mainstream, very pragmatic. She's not a threat to our Constitution. But third, that this is an important process. It's a transparent process.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: I'm so glad that the senators are doing their responsibility about the Constitution by asking tough questions, trying to see what a candidate thinks, trying to assure that they follow the law. But the reality is that nothing they do is going to assure that Republican or conservative, liberal or Democrat. But what they can do is let the American people know, I've done my job, carried out my duty, by asking important questions for someone who has an unprecedented lifetime on the court.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: So I do think they're doing their job. And I think that she's doing her job by letting us know that the law matters, not what I say, what I feel, but what I do and what I've done for the last 17 years.

Hmm. And by the way, we have been informed, when we just came on the air, Al Franken was quizzing Judge Sotomayor about Perry Mason cases. Indeed, he was asking about the case that Perry did not win, the only one. We've been informed it was the case of the deadly verdict from the 17th of October, 1963. But, of course, it was not Perry's fault. His client withheld evidence that Perry required to win. So, well, that was the one case that Perry Mason lost.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: Perry's still undefeated. That's…
Perry is still undefeated.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: I didn't know he'd lost one.
Indeed.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: He did one.

And I'm also told that indeed there were guest lawyers when Burr was recovering from surgery. That, of course, the actor who played Perry Mason, including Bette Davis in "The Case of the Constant Doyle" episode number 6-16 from 1963. David Savage, it's interesting we get such an interesting look into early 1960's television in the case of Judge Sotomayor. We're talking with Charles Ogletree and with Neomi Rao and, of course, David Savage. You're listening to Special Coverage from NPR News.

And, David, as you go back through this, we - so much of what we've been hearing in the last few days seems to be about these senators settling scores about what they - what was done properly and improperly in previous cases of Supreme Court nominees and, to some degree, marking the ground for the future.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: Yes. In the past, I recall mentioning to my colleagues in the office that this is sort of like them covering the Israelis and Palestinians. There's this endless long back and forth fight. And when you cover the Judiciary Committee, you always go up there and they start referring to the previous nominations, when your side did this and we did that and you held up the hearing or you filibustered or threatened - that seems to be the Judiciary Committee for a long time has been sort of an unhappy family.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: It is the - I have thought from the beginning that this hearing seems very much like the flipside of the Sam Alito hearing from two or three years ago. He was a well-qualified solid Appeals Court judge. The Republicans had a majority. You almost knew he was going to be confirmed. He basically explained his cases and didn't say much. The Democrats criticized him, voted against him; he was confirmed.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: This was a little bit the same. Sonia Sotomayor is an exceptionally well-qualified, competent, smart Appeals Court judge. The Republicans, you know, don't think that she's the person they'd like on the Supreme Court. The Democrats have a solid majority. She doesn't have to win over the Republican votes. She can just play defense for three days and she will be confirmed.
Speaking of winning over, Neomi Rao, is there anything that she could have said in the last couple of days that would have changed your mind?

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: Well, that's an interesting question. You know, I think that she's been like many nominees before the Judiciary Committee in the circumstances. She's been extremely deliberate. She's been careful. She's been cautious. And as David noted, she doesn't really have much to lose. And so, she can play defense.

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: And I think, you know, it's hard to say that something that happens over a couple of days can reflect a person's judicial philosophy more than, you know, over a decade on the Court of Appeals and a series of writings and speeches. So I think it would take a lot for me to view her record differently simply based on the statements that she made at the hearing.

And let me ask you the same question, almost in reverse, Charles Ogletree. You mentioned some of her decisions, you know, citing her prosecution background that give you pause. But nevertheless, is there something that would have disturbed you, do you think, that would have made you reconsider your support for the nominee?

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: I don't think so because my sense is that what she agrees with is within the bounds of the law. She's not making new law. She's affirming constitutional principles. And she believes, like she said today, that there's a warrant requirement and the police didn't meet it in one case. But there are exceptions to the warrant requirement. And one of the tests is reasonableness and that there's a good faith exception. She's right about that.

speaker_label: Mr. CHARLES OGLETREE (Professor, Harvard Law School)
text: And what she said and what she did in that case was side for the government, even though a lot of people thought that if they didn't have a warrant it was defective, that ends the ballgame. But I like the fact that she says she's careful, she's meticulous. She may not - she will not rule my way all the time or even most of the time. But you know what, I'm very comfortable with the fact that she understands the enormity of her role, and she'll do a great job as a Supreme Court justice.
All right. Charles Ogletree and Noemi Rao, we thank you both for your time today. Appreciate you coming into the studio.
David, before we let you go, the senators - well, there will be a second round of questions?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: Yes. That's what I understand. They were going to have a closed-door meeting for an hour, and then the second round is supposed to be 20 minutes. The Republicans have said they want to go ahead with the second round. I assume that'll carry things well into tomorrow.
And then on Friday, we could expect the panels of people brought up by both sides, the minority and the majority, to testify on behalf.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID SAVAGE (Journalist, The Los Angeles Times; Chicago Tribune)
text: That's also possible, it may be up Thursday afternoon.
Thursday. Will you be ready to go up on Thursday afternoon, Neomi?

speaker_label: Ms. NEOMI RAO (Professor, George Mason University School of Law)
text: My understanding from the staff is that they would like to wrap up Thursday evening if possible.

Well, in that case, I sit corrected. Thank you very much for your time. Neomi Rao is an assistant professor of law at George Mason University School of Law. Charles Ogletree, the Jesse Climenko professor of law at Harvard Law School and executive director of the Charles Hamilton Houston Institute for Race and Justice. And of course, David Savage covers the Supreme Court for the Los Angeles Times and the Chicago Tribune.
